1.note: Biblical names. Pathros (Isa 11:11, Jer 44:1) is Upper Egypt. Caphtor (Deut 2:23, Amos 9:7) was taken by medieval Jewish writers (Saadia, Benjamin of Tudela) to be Damietta in the Nile Delta. The two names rhyme.

2.note: Hos 13:15 "though he be fruitful among brothers (אַחִים)". Many read the word there as "reeds" (from אָחוּ, meadow grass), which suits the shade of the plants here. Literally "among brothers".

3.note: חֶבְרָה "company, fellowship" plays on the name Ḥever (חֶבֶר), whom the narrator has not yet recognized.

4.note: Obscure. The root דלח is used in Ezek 32:2, 32:13 of stirring up water; "streams" is a guess from that. The form may be corrupt.

5.note: No-amon (Nah 3:8) is Egyptian Thebes. Medieval Jewish writers took it to be Alexandria, which suits her boasts of the sea here.

6.note: Prov 8:30, said by Wisdom: "I was beside Him as an אָמוֹן" (a nursling, or a craftsman). The city explains her name No-amon by this word.

7.note: מִצְרַיִם is Egypt, and in medieval Hebrew also its capital Fustat-Cairo, which is the city meant here beside Alexandria.

8.note: Zeph 3:1 "Woe to her that is rebellious (מֹרְאָה) and defiled (נִגְאָלָה), the oppressing city", said of Jerusalem. Read here as "the rebel (city) is defiled"; "her sight is defiled" is also possible.

9.note: The words are from Ps 22:16; the sense follows Ps 137:5–6, "let my tongue cleave to my palate if I do not remember you": a curse on anyone who does not speak her praise.

10.note: A play on שְׁכֵנָה "neighbor" and שְׁכִינָה "Shekhinah", from the same root (dwell).

11.note: The rivers of Damascus in 2 Kgs 5:12: Abana (the written text אבנה; the read form אמנה, Amana) and Pharpar, usually identified with the Barada and the Aʿwaj.

12.he: הִשְׁכִּין כְּבוֹדוֹ תוֹךְ / חַדְרָךְ וְדַמֶּשֶׂק מְנוּחָתוֹ
12.note: Zech 9:1 "the word of the Lord is in the land of Hadrach, and Damascus is its resting place". Hadrach is a place near Hamath; the rabbis (Sifre Deut 1) also read the verse to say that Jerusalem will extend to Damascus.

13.note: Zobah (Aram-zobah, 2 Sam 8:3, 10:6) is Aleppo in medieval Hebrew.

14.note: Uncertain. Perhaps the Temple lamp kept in order (Exod 27:20–21, Lev 24:3–4, the verb ערך), or "the lamp of the battle line" (מַעֲרָכָה, battle array).

15.note: A play on לְבָנָה "white" and לְבָנָה "moon".

16.note: A play on רוֹפְאֵי "healers" and רְפָאִים, which also means "the shades, the dead" (Isa 26:14): "healers who heal", or "healers of the dead".

17.note: Joseph's dream, Gen 37:7. אִלְּמוּ "were bound" also sounds like "were struck dumb" (אִלֵּם, mute): when the other cities fell silent, Zobah stood up.

18.note: Ashur (Assyria); in medieval Hebrew usually Mosul, across the Tigris from Nineveh. Her speech plays on the name with אֹשֶׁר "happiness" and Leah's words at the naming of Asher (Gen 30:13).

19.note: גְּאוֹנִים "prides, eminences" is also the title of the Geonim, the heads of the Babylonian academies of Sura and Pumbedita.
